analysis.one_liner: Let the President temporarily freeze gasoline prices at pre-Katrina levels after the 2005 hurricane.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote and with no cosponsors, three weeks after Hurricane Katrina sent gas prices soaring.
analysis.plain_summary: Days after Hurricane Katrina shut down Gulf Coast refineries and sent gas prices jumping, Senator Carl Levin proposed letting the President freeze wholesale and retail gasoline prices at their August 27, 2005 levels — before the storm hit. Companies that violated the freeze could be fined up to three times what they gained. The freeze would end once fuel supplies recovered to pre-storm levels. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households facing a sudden spike in gasoline and heating fuel prices right after the storm, plus businesses whose costs rose with fuel prices. The freeze would have held pump prices at pre-hurricane levels until domestic fuel supply recovered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers hit by post-Katrina gas spikes

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have let the President freeze wholesale and retail gasoline and petroleum product prices at or below their levels on August 27, 2005, the last full day before Katrina made landfall [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that refinery shutdowns and lost transportation capacity caused 'massive price increases' that created 'severe hardships for millions of Americans' dependent on gasoline for daily necessities [S3].
Violators could be fined up to three times their gain, and the government could seek court injunctions to stop violations, giving the freeze enforcement teeth [S2] [S3].
The freeze was temporary by design: it would terminate automatically once the President found that domestic petroleum supply had recovered to its August 27, 2005 level [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel sellers, who would have had to absorb the difference between what the market would bear after the supply shock and the frozen price — forfeiting the sharp post-storm profit increase on every gallon sold until supplies recovered.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: Economists across the political spectrum generally warn that price ceilings on a scarce good cause shortages, rationing, and lines at the pump — a real risk when a hurricane had just cut refining capacity, which is exactly why such freezes are rare and were not adopted after Katrina.
The bill concentrated sweeping discretion in the President, who could set the freeze's terms, delegate enforcement to any agency, and decide when supplies had recovered enough to end it [S2] [S3].
A price freeze caps what consumers pay but does not create more fuel; without addressing the underlying supply shortfall, savings at the pump could have come at the cost of availability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a strictly temporary emergency window, holding prices at pre-disaster levels would have put the cost of a natural disaster's supply shock on an industry earning record margins rather than on consumers, and the bill's automatic termination when supply recovered limited the shortage risk. Still, the strongest honest objection stands: price controls during a genuine supply squeeze can produce shortages and lines, and the bill gave the President very broad power with little structure around how adjustments would work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 7, 2005, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor ever signed on.

narrative.text: Senator Carl Levin introduced the bill on September 7, 2005, days after Katrina had damaged Gulf Coast petroleum production and refining facilities and driven fuel prices sharply higher [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors over its lifetime [S4], and Congress adjourned without it ever reaching the floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel retailers who were capturing sharply higher post-Katrina prices were better off, since no freeze was ever put in place and they kept selling at post-storm prices. Consumers, meanwhile, continued paying the hurricane-inflated price at the pump for as long as it lasted.

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the President temporarily freeze gasoline prices at pre-Katrina levels.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and committee agendas in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Set the legislative agenda in the aftermath of Katrina and brought no price-freeze measure to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough to test support: it had one Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.note: Katrina cut refining capacity and sent fuel prices sharply higher, lifting producers' and refiners' revenue per gallon. A freeze at pre-storm prices would have taken that windfall away, which is the direct cost the bill would have imposed.
Retail and wholesale fuel prices were both covered by the freeze, capping margins during a period when pump prices were rising. Enforcement included fines up to three times the gain from violations.
